scenes.headline: How Lanyon proves a PDE solver before running it
scenes.sub: A neural proposer, a symbolic engine, and IEEE-754 floating point.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Primrose! Lanyon writes numerical solvers for partial differential equations, and proves them correct before a single simulation runs. Here's how.

scenes.label: The idea
scenes.text: Derive the solver and its proof from one spec, prove it against real floating-point arithmetic, and reject it before it ever runs.
scenes.say: The idea: derive the code and its proof from one specification, check the proof against the arithmetic the hardware really uses, and reject bad code before it ever runs.

steps.say: A neural proposer writes the solver as one specification, in a small domain-specific language.
The proof and the solver code are both expanded from that same spec, so proving one thing while running another is designed out.
A symbolic engine then asks: does the proof type-check, and do the kernels compile? No time-step needed.
If not, the spec is wrong, and the error goes straight back to the proposer. A bad solver never produces a number.

scenes.title: Floats are not the reals
scenes.say: Why the proof must respect floating point: it isn't real-number arithmetic.

parts.say: Every float addition rounds. So adding a and b first, then c,

parts.note: can differ from grouping the other way
parts.say: can give a different answer from adding b and c first.

parts.note: real-number algebra can prove the wrong program
parts.say: So a proof done in real-number algebra can be about a kernel that never rounds: a program that doesn't exist. Lanyon allows commutativity, never associativity.

scenes.label: fewer output tokens than frontier models, as Lanyon reports it
scenes.note: two simple linear PDEs, self-graded, not yet replicated
scenes.say: Lanyon reports twenty to two hundred and fifty times fewer output tokens. But that's on two simple linear problems, self-graded, and not yet replicated.

scenes.text: Prove code against the arithmetic the hardware actually uses, and a bad solver never produces a number.
scenes.mark: the arithmetic the hardware actually uses

recap: One spec expands into both proof and code
A symbolic gate checks before anything runs
Proofs respect float rounding, not the reals
scenes.say: To recap: one spec for code and proof, a gate before the run, and proofs that respect rounding.
